name: ARO-INHBE

lead: ARO-INHBE is an experimental RNA interference drug that targets the INHBE gene, which encodes a liver-derived protein involved in fat distribution. Appearance communities follow it for the idea of losing fat while preserving muscle, with a leaner waistline.

RNAi lowers production of a specific protein by silencing its gene, so the chain is less INHBE, a shift in fat distribution, then less harmful fat and a leaner midsection. A phase 1/2 study in 190 adults with obesity began in December 2024 and is no longer recruiting, and a phase 2 trial in 252 adults with fatty liver disease (MASH) is registered with a September 2026 start. No results have been posted.

paras: It is available only within clinical trials, in people with obesity with and without type 2 diabetes.
Human safety has not been reported. It is investigational and not available by prescription.

angle.text: ARO-INHBE is an RNAi drug that silences INHBE to shift how fat is distributed, aiming for a leaner midsection rather than just lower appetite. It is in early obesity trials, with no results available yet.

lead: ARO-INHBE is an investigational RNA interference (RNAi) therapy aimed at the INHBE gene, which encodes a liver-produced protein, activin E, involved in how the body distributes fat. It is being tested in people with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, and a trial in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is planned. It is not approved for any use anywhere.[1][2]

The appeal for people interested in body composition is the idea of lowering fat, especially fat stored around the abdomen and organs, while leaving lean tissue intact, so that the result is a leaner look rather than general weight loss. Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals, the developer, bases the rationale on human genetic data: people carrying loss-of-function INHBE variants are reported to have healthier fat distribution and a lower risk of metabolic disease such as type 2 diabetes.[3]

In January 2026 Arrowhead released interim company-reported results from the first-in-human study. In a small number of participants, serum activin E fell in a dose-dependent way, visceral fat fell, and total lean tissue rose after a single dose in the monotherapy part; a combination part with tirzepatide reported larger fat reductions than tirzepatide plus placebo, in groups of three to five participants.[3] The data are interim, not peer reviewed, and the company itself notes the groups are small.[3]

A first-in-human Phase 1/2 study in adults with obesity began on 4 December 2024 and is active but no longer recruiting, with an enrollment listed as 190, and a Phase 2 MASH trial of 252 adults is registered as not yet recruiting with a September 2026 start.[1][2] The ARO- prefix follows the naming convention for RNAi candidates in the pipeline of Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals, a Pasadena-based company founded in 2004 that focuses on RNAi therapies.[4]

paras: RNAi is a natural gene-silencing process. In therapeutic use, short interfering RNA (siRNA) is delivered to cells, loads into the RNA-induced silencing complex and directs it to cut the matching messenger RNA, so the target protein is not made.[5] All RNAi drugs approved so far address diseases that originate in the liver, using delivery approaches such as GalNAc conjugates or lipid nanoparticles; examples listed on Wikipedia include givosiran, lumasiran, vutrisiran and inclisiran.[5]

ARO-INHBE reduces hepatic expression of the INHBE gene and its secreted product, activin E. Arrowhead cites human genetics as the rationale: loss-of-function INHBE variants are linked to better fat distribution and a lower risk of metabolic disease such as type 2 diabetes.[3] A sister candidate from the same company, ARO-ALK7, silences ACVR1C in fat cells to reduce production of the ALK7 receptor, with a similar genetic rationale; the company says animal studies of it showed reduced body weight and fat mass with preserved lean muscle.[3]

The first-in-human study (AROINHBE-1001, NCT06700538) is a dose-escalating Phase 1/2a trial in up to 78 adults with obesity according to the company, with registry enrollment listed as 190. Part 1 tests single and multiple doses as monotherapy and Part 2 tests combination with tirzepatide. It started on 4 December 2024 and is active, not recruiting.[1][3]

In the January 2026 interim release, serum activin E fell in a dose-dependent manner (four participants per dose level), with a mean maximum reduction of 85 percent after a single dose at the highest level. In the monotherapy part, a single dose produced a mean visceral fat reduction of 9.9 percent, a mean relative liver fat reduction of 38 percent and a 3.6 percent increase in total lean tissue at week 16, and two doses produced a placebo-adjusted visceral fat reduction of 15.6 percent at week 24.[3]

In participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes receiving tirzepatide, the company reported weight loss of 9.4 percent at week 16 in the group that also received ARO-INHBE (n=4) versus 4.8 percent with tirzepatide plus placebo (n=5). At week 12 by MRI, visceral fat fell 23.2 percent versus 7.4 percent, total fat 15.4 percent versus 5.3 percent, and relative liver fat 76.7 percent versus 20 percent (three versus five participants). The company described this as roughly twofold greater weight loss and threefold greater fat reduction; the release itself notes that group sizes are very small, that the comparison across studies is not randomised head to head, and that data are interim and company-reported.[3]

A Phase 2 trial (NCT07859813) in adults with MASH, planned for 252 participants and a September 2026 start, is registered as not yet recruiting.[2] Web reports indicate that further data were presented at the EASL congress in May 2026, but those results were not reviewed for this article.

According to the interim release, the drug was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild treatment-emergent adverse events and none leading to discontinuation. Injection-site reactions were mild and self-limited, and one serious adverse event (a limb abscess) was managed with bedside drainage and judged unrelated to treatment. Gastrointestinal event rates were similar between the combination and tirzepatide alone, and no clinically significant trends appeared in liver enzymes, glycaemic indices or lipids.[3]

The registered programme spans obesity and a liver disease indication, indicating that the developer is exploring more than one use, and the company plans additional results in 2026.[1][2][3] Whether the compound changes body weight, fat distribution or liver fat durably in larger randomised trials has not yet been published in peer-reviewed form.

Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals is a publicly traded company headquartered in Pasadena, California, founded on 1 January 2004. It acquired Novartis's RNAi research and development portfolio in 2015, was renamed from Arrowhead Research Corporation in April 2016, and in October 2018 closed a license and collaboration agreement with Janssen for ARO-HBV.[4] Wikipedia's company article does not mention ARO-INHBE.[4]

timeline.event: Phase 1/2 first-in-human trial in obesity begins (4 December).[1]
Interim company data released on 6 January; Phase 2 MASH trial registered with a planned September start.[2][3]
